stem: An 8-month-old with fever and cough has a chest X-ray showing a rounded airspace opacity; which explanation best accounts for this appearance in young children?

options.text: AP films in young children magnify the heart and mediastinum
The interconnections between alveoli are less well developed, so pneumonia does not spread as readily
Pleural fluid layers laterally to the lung
Collapse is sharply demarcated and shifts towards the consolidation
A normal thymus creates a triangular sail sign in the upper mediastinum

explanation: Round pneumonia is the correct concept. In infants, the interconnections between alveoli are less well developed, so infection is less likely to spread widely and can appear as a rounded airspace opacity on chest X-ray.

citations.source: Louisa Leone MD3 2025 - Child and Adolescent Health - Study Notes.pdf
citations.title: Louisa Leone MD3 2025 - Child and Adolescent Health - Study Notes.pdf

optionExplanations.A: Incorrect because AP magnification can make the heart and mediastinum look larger, but it does not explain a rounded airspace opacity.
optionExplanations.B: Correct because less well developed interconnections between alveoli in young children limit spread of pneumonia, producing a rounded opacity.
optionExplanations.C: Incorrect because pleural fluid layering describes a pleural effusion, not a rounded intrapulmonary consolidation.
optionExplanations.D: Incorrect because collapse is associated with volume loss and shift towards the affected side, not the classic appearance of round pneumonia.
optionExplanations.E: Incorrect because the thymic sail sign is a normal mediastinal finding and does not explain a rounded lung opacity.
